$$
f(x)=\frac{{e}^{-|x/3|}}{6},\,x\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\, & x<0 \\ h(x),\, & x\ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that involves an absolute value, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x<0 \\ {\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t, & x\ge 0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ce55fccd-c2b9-544b-881d-b59a7e7c0f42"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{9}(x-1)(x-4),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

its cumulative distribution function is 

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0,\, & x<1 \\ h(x),\, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1,\, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $h(x).$" :question/worked-solution "Since our random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive only for $1\le x\le 4,$ the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ {\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

For the given probability density function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}(t-1)(t-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{x}-\frac{2}{9}({t}^{2}-5t+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={(-\frac{2}{27}{t}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{t}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}t)|}_{1}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x-(-\frac{2}{27}+\frac{5}{9}-\frac{8}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1 \\ -\frac{2}{27}{x}^{3}+\frac{5}{9}{x}^{2}-\frac{8}{9}x+\frac{11}{27}, & 1\le x\le 4 \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5340e926-2580-5f2f-bf08-46d25e342346"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

Let's compute the integrals.

- If $x\le 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{x}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{2}|}_{-\infty }^{x} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & ={\frac{{e}^{x/3}}{2}|}_{x=0} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =-{\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{2}|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{{e}^{-t/3}}{6}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}+(-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =1-\frac{{e}^{-x/3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the cumulative distribution function is given by

$$

$$"] ["question-2b70eaac-0c45-5da5-8a2f-2002d9071035" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-ce55fccd-c2b9-544b-881d-b59a7e7c0f42" :answer-field/id #uuid Given a continuous random variable $X,$ the CDF is the function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

If our random variable has the probability density function (or PDF) $f(x),$ then we have

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t) \, \textrm dt.
$$

Note that we use $f(t)dt$ in the integrand because $x$ serves as the upper limit of integration. 

For example, consider the random variable $X$ with the following PDF:

![](images/e7/e79c230f2b548c9280425f555f6d99a8f997e989289a05fb5f4584b656c4dcc8.svg)

Since $f(x)= 0$ for all $x < 0,$  we have

$$
F(x)  = \int_{-\infty}^x 0 \, \textrm dt = 0
$$

if $x<0.$

To compute the CDF for $x\geq 0,$  we integrate $f(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =0+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{2}{\pi (1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡t|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x-\frac{2}{\pi }(0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing our CDF as a function defined over the entire real line, we get

$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).

"681dc276-df96-5b4d-b26c-338d9da62b88" 17592186045417] [17592186134584 1063 17592186133729 17592186045417] [17592186135186 1064 "The cumulative distribution function (or CDF) of a continuous random variable is defined the same way as for a discrete random variable. 

Given a continuous random variable $X,$ the CDF is the function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

If our random variable has the probability density function (or PDF) $f(x),$ then we have

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x) = \int_{-\infty}^x f(t) \, \textrm dt.
$$

Note that we use $f(t)dt$ in the integrand because $x$ serves as the upper limit of integration. 

For example, consider the random variable $X$ with the following PDF:

![](images/e7/e79c230f2b548c9280425f555f6d99a8f997e989289a05fb5f4584b656c4dcc8.svg)

Since $f(x)= 0$ for all $x < 0,$  we have

$$
F(x)  = \int_{-\infty}^x 0 \, \textrm dt = 0
$$

if $x<0.$

To compute the CDF for $x\geq 0,$  we integrate $f(x)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}f(t)\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{0}^{x}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =0+{\int }_{0}^{x}\frac{2}{\pi (1+{t}^{2})}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡t|}_{0}^{x} \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x-\frac{2}{\pi }(0) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing our CDF as a function defined over the entire real line, we get

![](images/66/66b7bf54271075ae72fcf07fa4dc8573a94e97c2b2cc77680c0ec94b6053f360.svg)" 17592186045417] [17592186135186 1065 8364 17592186045417] [17592186135186 1066 #uuid "de1bbdf6-687d-537a-a6fe-03d9fafbe841" 17592186045417] [17592186135186 1067 "Introduction" 17592186045417] [17592186135187 1064 "When a random variable $X$ has a probability distribution function $f(x)$ that is strictly positive on the interval $a \leq x \leq b$ only, we have

- $P(X \leq x) = 0$ for $x < a,$ and

- $P(X \leq x) = 1$ for $x > b.$

In these cases, the cumulative distribution function takes the following form:

![](images/7a/7a64bac7c252a3f52fc92f6364edb5c66f31e47da28e78eeb0d069d894135700.svg)" 17592186045417] [17592186135187 1065 8365 17592186045417] [17592186135187 1066 #uuid "0794419f-6b72-568b-a787-d71121c8bcd9" 17592186045417] [17592186135187 1067 "Finding a CDF Given a PDF With Lower and Upper Bounds" 17592186045417] [17592186135188 1064 "As with discrete random variables, we can use the CDF of a continuous random variable to quickly compute a probability over an interval:

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = F(b) - F(a)
$$

For example, suppose that a random variable $X$ has the following CDF:

$$
F(x) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-x}}, \qquad -\infty < x < \infty.
$$

We can use the above CDF to quickly compute $P(0 \leq x \leq 1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0\le x\le 1) & =F(1)-F(0) \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{1+{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+{e}^{-1}}-\frac{1}{2} \\  & ≈0.231\end{aligned}
$$

Remember that for continuous random variables, it doesn't matter whether or not we include the endpoints of the interval, so we have

$$
P(0 \leq X \leq 1) = P(0 < X \leq 1) = P(0 \leq X < 1) = P(0 < X < 1) = 0.231.
$$

In general, for a continuous random variable $X,$ we have

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b) = F(b) - F(a).
$$" 17592186045417] [17592186135188 1065 8366 17592186045417] [17592186135188 1066 #uuid "e5203710-822b-55d4-9dfb-985bc4d41d6a" 17592186045417] [17592186135188 1067 "Using a CDF to Compute a Probability Over an Interval" 17592186045417]]}
